problem: Open-vocabulary feature-embedded maps (VLMap, LERF, OpenScene) are computationally heavy and need pre-exploration or offline mapping, so they cannot be used for real-time exploration of unknown environments. Single-scale features also cannot answer queries at different granularity (object vs. room).
motivation: Maps searchable with open-vocabulary queries would enable a broader range of tasks, but they must be built online while the robot explores. A single object or region has different semantics at different viewing scales (a sink vs. a kitchen), so multi-scale features are needed.
key_idea: Split each RGB image into patches at several scales, batch them through CLIP once, and attach each patch feature to the mean back-projected 3D point of that patch, giving an online, sparse, multi-scale CLIP feature map that supports both online object-goal navigation and offline retrieval.
insight: The multi-scale ablation shows that mid-sized scales help (single-scale SR 72.2-77.8; scales 1,0,-1 give 87.0) while very small patches hurt (scale -2 alone gives 51.9, and adding it lowers SR from 87.0 to 85.2). Sparse patch-level CLIP features are enough for navigation and far faster than pixel-level LSeg (about 60x faster). The paper attributes the SR gain over VLMap to fewer false positives: it heads for the max-similarity point rather than the nearest pixel-level match.
method: Multi-scale patching: patches of size s_i=2^i·S (scales i=[1,0,-1], S=224) are cropped from the RGB image, resized to the CLIP input size, and concatenated along the batch dimension so the CLIP image encoder runs once per frame.

3D point embedding: depth is back-projected with intrinsics K and transformed to world coordinates using the DROID-SLAM pose; the points in each patch are averaged to give one 3D location per patch, and (point, feature) tuples are accumulated over time.

Retrieval: the text query is encoded with the CLIP text encoder, cosine similarity is computed against all map features, and points with similarity above threshold θ (0.3 for ViT-B/32, 0.27 for ViT-L/14) are the goals.
Navigation system: DepthMapper builds a 2D obstacle map (5 cm cells) from depth and pose, and multi-goal A* plans to the retrieved goals.

Exploration fallback: if there is no goal or it is unreachable, the agent navigates to a distant dummy point (-50,-50) to explore; if that is blocked, θ is lowered by 0.001 repeatedly until a reachable goal is found.

Offline retrieval and multi-object goals: after exploration without a goal, the stored features are queried with arbitrary text, and sequential goals reuse the existing map or trigger further exploration.

setting.backbone: CLIP ViT-B/32 and ViT-L/14 (frozen) + pretrained DROID-SLAM for pose + A* planner
setting.observation: egocentric RGB-D 640x480 (pose estimated by DROID-SLAM from RGB-D)
setting.action_space: 2D grid path following via multi-goal A* on an obstacle map (discrete navigation actions)
setting.simulator: Habitat (Matterport Pro2 scanned model house) + real robot
setting.privileged: none (simulator position and rotation are noted as observable; real robot uses DROID-SLAM)

numbers_note: All benchmarks are custom (own Habitat model houses), not standard benchmarks. The real-robot experiment is qualitative only.
results: With ViT-L/14 the method reaches SR 87.0 on custom Habitat object-goal navigation, versus VLMap 50.0, Detic 29.6 and YOLOv8 25.9, and even ViT-B/32 (64.8) beats VLMap. Mapping plus retrieval takes about 0.12 s (ViT-L/14) or 0.02 s (ViT-B/32) versus 7.0 s for an online VLMap. In multi-object navigation it reaches the 4th subgoal in 37 episodes vs 14 for VLMap. Offline P@1 (83.3) is comparable to VLMap-Normalized (85.2).
limitations: Maps are sparse (patch-level), which is insufficient for tasks needing centimeter-level goals such as picking.
Navigating to the max-likelihood point may skip the nearest object and lengthen paths, and threshold tuning trades off against false positives.
Evaluation is on small custom simulated scenes (54 and 100 episodes), and the real-robot test is a qualitative demo.
